leadRef: Lean community certifies AI-assisted Riemann Hypothesis proof as correct
description: The Lean community certifies Levent Alpöge's AI-assisted proof of the Riemann Hypothesis; OpenAI's chief scientist proposes shared industry limits measured by perplexity; OpenRouter drops three AI providers after researchers catch prompt and key theft; California adds a criminal angle to the Nvidia probe.

thirtySecond.p: Chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposes labs agree caps, measured by pretraining perplexity, until AI monitoring catches up.
Researchers found attackers inside three AI hosting providers; OpenRouter dropped them and pulled 125 endpoints from zero-data-retention.
California's attorney general says his Nvidia investigation covers possible criminal violations; hearings follow on 1-2 Dec.

footerNote: Monday's deep beat, research and AI models: two days after release, the Lean community certified an AI-assisted proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, and OpenAI published its pretraining loss curve with a call for shared limits. The model scan found no new architecture release: Inkling 2 Mini dominates Hugging Face and OpenRouter, while NVIDIA's Nemotron-Labs-Sigma diffusion LMs and Kimi K3.1 Pro are older releases.

stories.title: The Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative, certify (21 Nov) that Levent Alpöge's 17-million-line Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, released 20 Nov and built with an internal Claude model, is correct: dozens reproduced the build, two independent tools confirmed it proves exactly Mathlib's statement, and several independent proof checkers accepted it; MIT's Andrew Sutherland, running checks with Claude Code, reports all 175,187 modules compile with only the three standard axioms
stories.h: Lean community certifies AI-assisted Riemann Hypothesis proof as correct after independent checks
stories.sub: Two days after Levent Alpöge released a 17-million-line machine-checked proof built with Claude, the people who maintain Lean say the statement and the proof are both right.
stories.ticker: Lean and Mathlib communities certify Alpöge's Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis; 175,187 modules compile, independent checkers accept
stories.body:
The Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative, published a joint statement on 21 Nov: "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct." The proof, released on 20 Nov as a Lean library of 17 million lines, depends only on Mathlib. Dozens of people rebuilt it and got the same proof export; the community isolated Mathlib's own statement of the hypothesis and two separate tools (comparator and con-leche) confirmed the library proves exactly that; and several proof checkers, including Lean's kernel and checkers written in other languages, accepted the exported proof. Two of them (con-leche, con-ron) come with a formal proof that they cannot accept a false proof. MIT's Andrew Sutherland, who ran his checks with Claude Code, reports all 175,187 modules compile, the five headline theorems use only the three standard axioms, and a sandboxed rebuild reproduced the 61.6GB export byte for byte; two checks were still running on 22 Nov. Metaculus forecasters had expected a proof around 2035.

So what: machine-checked AI-assisted proofs are now trusted by the people who run the checker, within two days. Expect the same pattern (AI writes, a formal checker certifies) in software, smart contracts and risk models; the open question is understanding the new ideas, not whether they are right.

stories.brief: On 20 Nov Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working with an internal Claude model, released a Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, the 1859 conjecture about how prime numbers are distributed. On 21 Nov the communities that build Lean and its maths library certified it: the statement is Mathlib's own, the code compiles for everyone who tried, and independent checkers accept the proof. Mathematicians still have to understand the new ideas inside it.

stories.title: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposes (22 Nov) that labs adopt perplexity (pretraining loss) as a shared progress metric and agree common limits they will not cross until monitoring reaches a concrete milestone, such as a successor to chain-of-thought monitors; OpenAI publishes its own curve (GPT-3.5 ~0.99 log-perplexity, GPT-4 ~0.91, now below 0.8; a ~0.76 model started producing breakthrough maths results) and warns of an 'avalanche' of AI-driven pretraining advances as soon as 2027; Sam Altman backs it (Reuters)
stories.h: OpenAI's chief scientist asks rival labs to agree shared limits on AI pretraining progress
stories.sub: Jakub Pachocki publishes OpenAI's internal perplexity curve and proposes a cross-lab cap until monitoring catches up.
stories.ticker: OpenAI's Pachocki proposes common industry limits measured by perplexity; Altman backs it
stories.body:
In a post titled Perplexity and Intelligence, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki argues that pretraining loss (perplexity) is the best single measure of how capable a model's base is, and publishes OpenAI's internal numbers: GPT-3.5 at ~0.99 log-perplexity, GPT-4 at ~0.91, and recent models below 0.8, where 'transformative capabilities' in cybersecurity and maths appeared. A model at ~0.76 'started producing groundbreaking results' on open maths problems. He expects more as models reach 0.68-0.7, warns AI could set off an 'avalanche' of pretraining advances as soon as 2027, and says alignment auditing will likely get worse. He proposes common limits, 'based on perplexity and other measurements', that developers commit not to cross until monitoring reaches a concrete milestone, such as a successor to chain-of-thought monitors. Reuters reports Sam Altman backs the proposal; no response yet from other labs.

So what: this is the first frontier lab to publish its own pretraining curve and ask for a cross-industry cap. Whether Anthropic, Google and xAI sign up decides if it becomes a standard regulators can point to, as Democrats prepare to make AI oversight a priority in the new Congress.
stories.chip: OpenAI's post opened (numbers and proposal quoted from it); Reuters copy on Yahoo opened for Altman's backing
src: Reuters via Yahoo: OpenAI scientist proposes industry AI limits
stories.short: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposes that labs track pretraining perplexity as a shared measure and agree limits they will not cross until monitoring improves. OpenAI publishes its curve: GPT-4 at about 0.91, recent models below 0.8, and a 0.76 model producing breakthrough maths results. He warns of rapid AI-driven pretraining advances as soon as 2027. Altman backs it.

stories.title: After Dragos researchers seeded ~2 million prompts with canary AWS keys and URLs (Jul-Nov 2026) and found attackers stealing requests at three AI hosting providers, resellers on an inference marketplace reading prompts, and privacy settings ignored (prompts sent to Chinese firms), OpenRouter says (22 Nov) it has off-boarded three providers, removed 125 endpoints from zero-data-retention eligibility and notified affected customers; Together, Novita (MiniMax requests), Phala and Atlas Cloud have posted notices
stories.h: OpenRouter drops three AI providers after researchers catch prompts and keys being stolen
stories.sub: Dragos seeded two million prompts with fake AWS keys; attackers used them within a day, and 'zero data retention' flags did not stop it.
stories.ticker: OpenRouter off-boards 3 inference providers, pulls 125 endpoints from zero-data-retention after Dragos canary study
stories.body:
Dragos (research led by HD Moore) sent about two million prompts containing unique URLs and canary AWS credentials to AI services from July to November. It found attackers inside three hosting providers, copying requests 'at the provider's front door'; in the largest case every request sent in late-October windows was stolen, a couple of hundred AWS keys were tested within hours and used for tens of thousands of API calls, including attempts to enable Bedrock models and add IAM users. Some stolen requests were flagged zero-data-retention. Separately, resellers on an inference marketplace could read and keep customer prompts using ordinary logging, and some providers sent prompts to Chinese companies against their stated policies. OpenRouter says no breach of its own systems, but it has off-boarded three providers, removed 125 endpoints from ZDR eligibility, notified affected customers and will run similar canary tests continuously. Together, Novita, Phala and Atlas Cloud have published notices.

So what: a 'privacy' flag binds only the first hop. Banks routing prompts through model marketplaces should pin providers, keep credentials out of prompts and agent context, and treat any key that went through a third-party inference provider since July as exposed.
stories.chip: OpenRouter's announcement opened (three providers off-boarded, 125 endpoints, provider notices); Dragos research post opened (method and findings)
src: OpenRouter: Data processing incidents on inference providers

stories.short: Dragos seeded about two million prompts with fake AWS keys and found attackers inside three AI hosting providers, using stolen keys within hours, even on zero-data-retention requests. Marketplace resellers could also read prompts. OpenRouter has off-boarded three providers, pulled 125 endpoints from zero-data-retention and notified customers; it says its own systems were not breached.

stories.title: Monday 23 Nov: Korea's Kospi falls a further ~3.1% to about 4,718 in early trade while US stock futures rebound (Nasdaq 100 futures +2.9%, S&P 500 futures +2.1%, Dow futures about +690 points) after Friday's correction; Taiwan's regulator bans most short selling from today, raises short-sale margin to 150% and halts new put warrants after the Taiex's 17.5% weekly fall, its worst since 1991; Japan is closed for a holiday; bitcoin is back near $61,000
stories.h: Kospi slides again as US futures bounce and Taiwan bans most short selling
stories.ticker: Kospi ~-3% to 4,718 early; Nasdaq 100 futures +2.9%; Taiwan short-selling ban starts; BTC ~$61K
stories.body:
Asia opened the week still selling. Market data show the Kospi at about 4,718 shortly after the open, down about 3.1% from Friday's 4,869.96 (Korean outlets reported it slipping below 4,900 at the open). In New York, futures pointed the other way: Nasdaq 100 futures were up about 2.9%, S&P 500 futures about 2.1% and Dow futures about 690 points early on Monday in Asia. Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission decided on 21 Nov to ban short sales of most stocks that have already fallen, from today, lift the short-sale margin requirement from 130% to 150% and halt new put warrant applications, its first broad ban since 2015, after the Taiex lost 17.5% in the week to 36,033.29. Tokyo is shut for Labour Thanksgiving Day. Bitcoin traded near $61,100, up from Friday's low of $57,716.

So what: a futures bounce is not a bottom; Taiwan's ban removes a hedge for funds holding Taiwanese chip stocks, and Korean retail margin debt is the next pressure point. Watch Nvidia's first session after the SEC and California probes.

stories.title: A New York state judge hears on Monday (23 Nov, 11:30am ET) Attorney General Letitia James's request for a temporary restraining order against Kalshi, which says the order would force it to shut its exchange for all customers because it is headquartered in New York; the case returned to state court after a federal judge ruled on 19 Nov and a Manhattan federal judge on 20 Nov rejected the CFTC's second emergency bid to halt it; James seeks up to $36bn
stories.h: Kalshi faces New York hearing it says could shut its exchange nationwide
stories.ticker: NY judge hears AG's bid to restrain Kalshi today; CFTC's second emergency bid rejected
stories.body:
New York's attorney general wants an order barring Kalshi from running what she calls unlicensed gambling 'within or from New York', restricting trading by under-21s and banning campus advertising. Kalshi's lawyers say that because the exchange is based in New York the order would force it to stop serving all clients and possibly liquidate every open position; the AG says she does not intend to shut its national business. The case was sent back to the New York County Supreme Court on 19 Nov, and on 20 Nov a federal judge in Manhattan rejected the CFTC's second emergency request to stop it. The suit, filed 31 Jul, seeks up to $36bn in restitution and penalties, more than Kalshi's reported $22bn valuation. This was held back on 21 Nov because the sources could not be opened.

So what: this is the sharpest test yet of whether states can police federally regulated event contracts; brokers and banks building prediction-market products (Coinbase plans its own in 2027) should watch the order's scope.

stories.title: South Korea's education minister Choi Kyo-jin resigns (22 Nov) after AI-assisted cheating fears upended the suneung university entrance exam: the top scorer on the national tax accountant exam confessed to photographing questions with a hidden camera and reading AI answers from a phone, prompting wifi blocks, doubled supervisors, button stickers and a reward of at least $75,000 for reports; President Lee accepts; the ministry widens its probe to past exams
stories.h: South Korea's education minister resigns over AI cheating scandal around national exams
stories.ticker: Korean education minister Choi Kyo-jin resigns after AI-assisted cheating scandal
stories.body:
Choi Kyo-jin, 72, resigned saying he takes 'full responsibility' for failing to prepare, after a week in which the top scorer on Korea's national tax accountant exam admitted he photographed the questions with a concealed micro-camera, sent them to an AI system and read the answers from a smartphone. Four days later 500,000-plus students sat the suneung under emergency rules: public wifi blocked near test sites, twice as many supervisors, pencils only, stickers over clothing buttons that could hide cameras, and a reward of at least $75,000 for reporting cheating. Choi had told parliament that 'due to my age' he was not confident cheaters could be caught. The Guardian and BBC report the exam passed without major incidents; Korean media say the ministry is extending its investigation to past suneung exams.

So what: high-stakes testing, including professional certification such as banking and accounting exams, now has to assume a hidden camera and a frontier model; expect a move to supervised digital testing and oral checks.
stories.chip: The Guardian opened (confession, measures, resignation quote); BBC and Korean outlets seen in the collector
src: The Guardian: South Korean minister quits after AI cheating scandal

stories.short: South Korea's education minister resigned after AI-assisted cheating fears upended the national university exam. The top scorer on the tax accountant exam confessed to using a hidden camera and AI answers on a phone, prompting wifi blocks, doubled supervisors and rewards of at least $75,000 for reports. The exam itself passed without major incidents.

stories.title: COP31 in Turkey ends (22 Nov) without a major new climate deal after the longest UN climate conference ever: the final text never mentions fossil fuels, the EU, Pacific islands, Panama and others object, poorer countries get no clear adaptation finance; UN chief Guterres says he is 'deeply disappointed'; the BBC says a main COP deal last collapsed like this in Copenhagen in 2009
stories.h: COP31 climate talks end without a major deal after row over fossil fuels
stories.ticker: COP31 ends with no major deal; final text omits fossil fuels; Guterres 'deeply disappointed'
stories.body:
Talks in Antalya were due to end on Friday but ran into Sunday, making this the longest UN climate conference on record. A draft presented early on Sunday did not contain the words 'fossil fuels', only a nod to the COP28 pledge to 'transition away' from them. The EU's negotiator, Irish minister Darragh O'Brien, said it went 'nowhere near' the ambition needed; Panama and the Marshall Islands also objected, and poorer countries complained of no clear money from richer nations for adaptation. António Guterres, at his last COP, blamed 'powerful fossil fuel interests'. In Australia, which hosts negotiations next year, the Liberals demanded energy minister Chris Bowen resign over the outcome. A storage alliance with CATL, BYD and ACWA was launched on the sidelines.

So what: with no new multilateral push, climate policy shifts back to national rules and markets; for banks that means more weight on EU and UK disclosure rules and on physical-risk pricing, not on a global carbon pathway.
stories.chip: BBC report opened (final text, objections, Guterres quotes); Guardian Australia and pv magazine headlines seen in the collector
src: BBC: COP31 fails to reach major climate deal
stories.short: COP31 in Turkey ended on Sunday without a major new climate deal after the longest UN climate talks ever. The final text never mentions fossil fuels; the EU, Pacific islands and others objected, and poorer countries got no clear adaptation money. Guterres said he was deeply disappointed; the BBC compares it to Copenhagen in 2009.

stories.title: Democrats reach at least 258 US House seats (22 Nov) after Chuck Hubbard's recount win over Virginia Foxx in North Carolina, their largest majority since 1992, setting up divided government with the Senate also Democratic; leaders plan a 100-day cost-of-living agenda and broad oversight of Trump; Hakeem Jeffries says he will move 'very early' to ban lawmakers from trading stocks
stories.h: Democrats win biggest House majority since 1992, setting up a divided government
stories.ticker: Democrats win at least 258 House seats, largest majority since 1992
stories.body:
With Chuck Hubbard's victory in North Carolina after a recount, Democrats hold at least 258 of 435 House seats to Republicans' at least 173, the most for the party since 1992 (258) and 2008 (257). The Senate is also Democratic, so President Trump faces a divided Congress from January. Democrats say they will pass a 100-day agenda on living costs and run extensive oversight; Hakeem Jeffries says a ban on lawmakers trading stocks will come 'very early'. AI is on the list: a Democratic lawmaker told The Hill the next Congress will focus on AI in healthcare, jobs and agriculture, and the Senate passed a data-centre permitting and grid-cost bill last week.

So what: the incoming House controls appropriations and investigations; expect hearings on AI chip exports, Nvidia, the tech outages and data-centre power costs, and slower deregulation of banks and crypto.

stories.title: E-commerce and subscription billing platform Cleverbridge, used by software firms including Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Sony and Parallels, says hackers copied payment card data stored on its platform; it detected the intrusion on 4 Nov and began notifying customers on 20 Nov; notifications seen by BleepingComputer say card numbers, expiry dates and CVV codes were taken (reported 22 Nov)
stories.h: Software billing firm Cleverbridge says hackers stole card numbers and CVV codes
stories.ticker: Cleverbridge breach: card numbers, expiry dates and CVVs stolen; notifications began 20 Nov
stories.body:
Cleverbridge sells software and subscriptions on behalf of vendors such as Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Sony and Parallels. It says it spotted unauthorised activity on 4 Nov, took systems offline and brought them back the same day, but later found a third party had copied payment card data stored on the platform. It began notifying affected buyers on 20 Nov; a notice seen by BleepingComputer lists card number, expiry date and CVV/CVC. It has not said how many cards or which vendors' customers are affected. Storing CVVs after authorisation is barred under PCI DSS.

So what: card issuers should expect fraud on cards used for software purchases since early November and consider reissuing; merchants of record are a concentrated target, and this one apparently held the security codes that should never be kept.

stories.title: GL.iNet confirms (advisory 20 Nov, reported 22 Nov) that attackers exploited a flaw in its GoodCloud remote-management service to install malware on customers' routers and KVM devices, with some users reporting backdoors and reverse shells; the cloud flaw is fixed but already-infected devices stay infected; it has not said how many customers were hit or whether computers attached to KVMs were compromised
stories.h: Hackers used GL.iNet's cloud service to plant malware on routers and KVM devices
stories.ticker: GL.iNet cloud flaw used to infect routers and KVMs; patch blocks new infections only
stories.body:
GL.iNet makes home and travel routers and KVM-over-IP devices that let admins control servers remotely. Its GoodCloud platform manages them remotely, and the company says an unauthorised party exploited a vulnerability there to install malicious software. 'The attack path has been blocked,' it says, but the fix 'does not remove malware from devices that were already infected'. It told users to look for a process running as crond -i /tmp/.log and install the latest security firmware; it has not said how many devices were hit, and is investigating whether computers attached to infected KVMs were compromised. The advisory reached the Hacker News front page.

So what: KVM devices sit below every endpoint control; anyone who used GoodCloud to reach servers or branch machines should treat attached hosts as possibly compromised and check for the indicator.
stories.chip: BleepingComputer opened; GL.iNet's security notice opened (indicator and remediation)

stories.short: GL.iNet says attackers exploited a flaw in its GoodCloud remote-management service to install malware on customers' routers and KVM devices, with some users finding backdoors. The cloud hole is closed but infected devices stay infected. It has not said how many were hit or whether servers attached to KVMs were compromised.

stories.title: The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of the National Crime Information Center database used for warrants and background checks (reported 21-22 Nov); Trump says 'it's not good'; it follows the 20 Nov firing of White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross after a string of US outages that hit banking and air traffic control, with Pentagon CIO Kirsten Davies named as his replacement; on 22 Nov a Delta weight-and-balance system failure delayed all its Atlanta flights
stories.h: FBI investigates apparent crime-database hack days after White House fires its cyber chief
stories.ticker: FBI probes apparent NCIC breach; national cyber director Cairncross fired; Delta Atlanta outage
stories.body:
US media report the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of the National Crime Information Center, which federal and local police use for warrants and background checks; the FBI did not comment, and Trump said he had 'just heard' about it. On 20 Nov the White House removed National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, after he lost the confidence of chief of staff Stephen Miller (CBS); Marco Rubio named Pentagon CIO Kirsten Davies as successor. The removal follows last week's outages across banking, the FAA and Microsoft, which officials say were not cyberattacks. On Sunday a failure of Delta's weight-and-balance system delayed every Delta flight at Atlanta, a week after the FAA groundstop.

So what: the US government's cyber leadership is changing while a criminal-justice database may be exposed; banks that rely on NCIC-derived background checks should watch for guidance, and operational-resilience teams should expect more scrutiny after the outage run.

stories.short: The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center, the database police use for warrants and background checks. Two days earlier the White House fired cyber director Sean Cairncross after outages that hit banks and air traffic control. On Sunday a Delta system failure delayed every Delta flight at Atlanta.

stories.title: China's securities regulator has told law firms it will not approve offshore listings by red-chip companies set up after its 2023 offshore-listing rules unless they re-domicile in China, Reuters reports (sources, 20-22 Nov), tightening control over capital raised abroad and threatening Hong Kong's IPO pipeline as China's AI stocks slump
stories.h: China to bar young 'red-chip' firms from listing abroad unless they move home
stories.ticker: Reuters: CSRC to block offshore listings by red-chip firms set up after 2023 unless re-domiciled
stories.body:
Red-chip companies are registered abroad, usually in tax havens, but control businesses in China; the structure is favoured by tech start-ups listing in Hong Kong or New York. Reuters, citing people familiar, says the China Securities Regulatory Commission told law firms in recent days that red-chip companies established after the 2023 offshore-listing rules must re-domicile in China before listing offshore. The guidance is confidential and unannounced. It comes as China's AI stocks slump; the collector also carried a report that Chinese AI shares have lost about $1.7 trillion, which we could not open.

So what: Hong Kong's IPO boom depends on mainland tech; investment banks' Asia ECM pipelines and venture exits for Chinese AI start-ups just got narrower.
stories.chip: Reuters report opened via Mint; the CSRC has made no public statement
src: Reuters via Mint: Beijing to bar young red-chip firms from listing outside mainland
stories.short: China's securities regulator has told law firms it will not approve offshore listings by red-chip companies set up after 2023 unless they move their domicile to China, Reuters reports, citing sources. The unannounced guidance tightens control of capital raised abroad and could dent Hong Kong's IPO pipeline as Chinese AI stocks slump.

stories.title: A suspected drone attack sets fire to a Russian ship at Benghazi naval base, Libya (22 Nov); satellite firm Vantor says imagery shows a Steregushchiy-class corvette capsized and sunk with only its bow visible; a commercial ship off Benghazi is also hit; a day earlier the sanctioned Russian cargo ship Sparta II was struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland, and Finland's defence forces say Ukraine was likely behind it
stories.h: Drones hit Russian ships in Libya and the Gulf of Finland, sinking a corvette
stories.ticker: Russian corvette appears sunk at Benghazi after suspected drone strike; Sparta II hit in Gulf of Finland
stories.body:
Libya's eastern government says an explosion at dawn on Sunday on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base, stopped for fuel on its way home, was a suspected drone attack, with no casualties; BBC Verify geolocated video of the ship in flames. US-based Vantor says images show a Project 20380 (Steregushchiy-class) corvette moored on Saturday and capsized and sunk on Sunday. A commercial vessel off Benghazi was also hit, with minor injuries. Moscow has not commented. On Saturday the US- and Ukraine-sanctioned cargo ship Sparta II, bound for Kaliningrad, was hit by two drones in the eastern Gulf of Finland, caught fire and drifted into Finnish waters; Finland's defence forces say Ukraine was likely responsible. It follows Poland's report on 20 Nov of a Russian missile landing on its soil.

So what: the sea war is spreading to the Mediterranean and the Baltic, raising marine war-risk premiums and sanctions-enforcement questions for shipping finance.
stories.chip: BBC reports opened for both attacks (Libyan government statement, Vantor imagery, Finnish defence forces)

stories.short: A suspected drone attack set a Russian ship on fire at Libya's Benghazi naval base on Sunday; satellite images show a Russian corvette capsized and sunk. A day earlier drones hit the sanctioned Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland, and Finland says Ukraine was likely behind it. Moscow has not commented.

stories.title: OneMain Financial wins Utah and FDIC approval (announced last week, analysed 22 Nov) for OneMain Bank, an industrial loan company that must hold at least $341m of paid-in capital and a 15% leverage ratio; the branchless bank will originate personal loans, auto loans and credit cards through OneMain's 1,300+ storefronts, let it offer a uniform product nationwide at up to 36% APR instead of state licences, and bring its BrightWay card in-house from WebBank
stories.h: FDIC approves OneMain's industrial bank, letting it lend nationwide at up to 36%
stories.ticker: FDIC approves OneMain Bank ILC: $341m capital, 15% leverage; uniform 36% APR lending
stories.body:
Twenty months after applying, OneMain has approval from Utah's Department of Financial Institutions and deposit insurance from the FDIC for OneMain Bank, an industrial loan company. Per the FDIC order, it must raise at least $341m of paid-in capital and keep a 15% leverage ratio; as an ILC owner OneMain avoids becoming a bank holding company but signs a parent company agreement giving the FDIC oversight. The bank will originate unsecured and auto loans and credit cards, funded mainly by brokered deposits, and sell most of them to OneMain, which will distribute them through 1,300+ storefronts in 44 states. The charter lets it replace state-by-state licensing with a single product nationwide at up to 36% APR, and issue its BrightWay card itself instead of through WebBank. It expects to be operating in about a year. Fintech Business Weekly asks whether Dave can follow where Enova and OppFi did not.

So what: it continues the fintech-charter wave (OakNorth, Payoneer, MoonPay this month); sponsor banks such as WebBank lose programmes, and consumer-lending competition at the 36% ceiling grows.

So what: a softer cap protects issuer economics for Mexican banks and card networks while still compressing merchant fees over time.

stories.title: A Uniphore preprint (19 Nov) using AppSci-Bench, seven simulated business workflows such as invoice review and airline rebooking, finds AI agent builders grade their own work near-perfect (86 of 132 builds scored at least 99% on self-written tests) while gains on withheld cases are small (13 Claude Opus 4.8 builds: +16.9 points on own tests, +3.2 on held-out); turning the test-and-revise loop on or off made no significant difference across 252 builds
stories.h: AI agent builders ace their own tests but barely improve on hidden cases
stories.ticker: Uniphore: 86 of 132 AI-built agents scored 99%+ on own tests; held-out gains small
stories.body:
Researchers at Uniphore had AI builders create business agents in seven simulated workflows and then scored them on cases held back during development. 86 of 132 builds with self-tests scored at least 99% on tests they wrote; in 13 Claude Opus 4.8 builds, revisions raised own-test scores by 16.9 points but held-out scores by only 3.2. Benchmark code and results are released.

So what: if your AI-built agents for operations or compliance are validated only by tests the same AI wrote, you are measuring confidence, not quality; keep independent held-out cases.

stories.title: Builders: pequalnp.com runs a coordinated fleet of volunteers' AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI) on P vs NP, each assigned one open step and checked in Lean, with a live viewer (86 HN points); and a Show HN game casts the player as an LLM's subagent (265 points); a separate group maps progress on formalising Masullo's human GRH manuscript in Lean
stories.h: Builders point volunteer AI agent fleets at P vs NP, with Lean checking every step
stories.body:
pequalnp.com hands each visiting agent session one open lemma; every proof goes through the same Lean checker, and a live board weights lines of attack toward P = NP or P ≠ NP by checked lemmas (it stresses this is not a probability). On Hacker News, a Show HN game where you play an LLM's subagent reached 265 points, and a progress map for formalising Alessandro Masullo's competing all-human GRH manuscript in Lean reached 106.

So what: the copyable idea is the pattern: split a big problem into checkable units, let anyone's agent take one, and accept only machine-verified results.

stories.title: Google previews 'semantic governance policies' on its Gemini platform: an LLM judge at an enforcement point such as Agent Gateway checks each tool call an agent proposes against the user's request and company rules and blocks it before it runs, a guard against indirect prompt injection (Help Net Security, 23 Nov)
stories.h: Google previews checks that block an AI agent's tool call before it runs
stories.ticker: Google previews semantic governance: LLM judge blocks agent tool calls breaking policy
stories.body:
The check sits outside the agent. A language model compares each proposed tool call with the user's request and written policies, so an agent talked out of its instructions by a user or a poisoned document is still stopped at the gateway. It is in preview.

So what: this is the control pattern regulators will expect for agentic banking: policy enforced outside the model, at the action.

stories.update: California's attorney general confirms a probe that includes possible criminal violations of state law over Nvidia's China chip sales and statements to investors; Shopify's Tobi Lütke calls Nvidia's board 'knuckleheads' as a petition for Huang's return passes 100,000 signatures; congressional hearings are set for 1-2 Dec
stories.title: California Attorney General Rob Bonta says (Bloomberg interview, 20 Nov) his investigation into whether Nvidia illegally sold advanced chips to China and misled investors includes possible criminal violations of state law, alongside the SEC accounting probe; Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke calls the board that accepted Jensen Huang's 12 Nov resignation 'knuckleheads' and backs a petition for his return (100,000+ signatures); the board, under interim CEO Colette Kress, has refused; congressional hearings are scheduled for 1-2 Dec; the WSJ reports a third figure, Li Ming, ran the Megaspeed network
stories.h: California opens criminal angle on Nvidia's China chip sales as pressure to reinstate Huang grows
stories.ticker: California AG probe of Nvidia includes possible criminal violations; hearings 1-2 Dec
stories.body:
Rob Bonta told Bloomberg the state is looking at 'prohibitions in California law, both civil and criminal, against misleading investors and the public', and at whether Nvidia or former CEO Jensen Huang gave false information about sales to China. The probe was prompted partly by Huang's affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive US intelligence suspects of spying; Megaspeed bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips. It runs alongside the SEC accounting investigation (now including Nvidia's 2025 switch from billing-address to headquarters-based geographic revenue reporting, which removed Singapore as a separate line) and a DOJ export-control inquiry. Shopify's Tobi Lütke used a 22 Nov podcast to call the directors 'knuckleheads'; a petition for Huang's return has passed 100,000 signatures, but the board, which named Colette Kress interim CEO, has refused. Congressional hearings on Nvidia's leadership are set for 1-2 Dec. The WSJ reports that Li Ming, a partner of Alice Huang and her husband Kang Wei, ran the network that moved chips to China (paywalled; not opened). Nvidia closed Friday at $125.53.

So what: a state criminal angle raises the stakes for Nvidia's executives and directors and for lenders with Nvidia exposure; the 1-2 Dec hearings and Nvidia's delayed 10-Q are the next dates.
